content: Trench fever is an infectious disease characterized by intermittent episodes of fever, chills, and an enlarged spleen (splenomegaly). Each episode can last up to 40 hours. The causative agent of this disease is Bartonella quintana, and it is transmitted to humans through the human body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis). Historically, trench fever was a significant problem during World War I and World War II. It affected soldiers in various regions, including Flanders, France, Poland, Galicia, Italy, Salonika, Macedonia, Mesopotamia, and Egypt during World War I. Notably, J.R.R. Tolkien was among those infected. Between 1915 and 1918, trench fever accounted for illnesses in one-fifth to one-third of British troops and about one-fifth of German and Austrian troops. During World War II, the disease also impacted the German army in Russia. The pathophysiology of trench fever involves the transmission of Bartonella quintana through contamination of skin abrasions or louse-bite wounds with the feces of an infected body louse. In some cases, the infection may also be directly transmitted through the bite of an infected louse. The causative organism, Bartonella quintana, resides in the stomach walls of the body louse. This bacterium is closely related to other pathogenic microbes, such as those responsible for Rocky Mountain spotted fever and typhus. Epidemiologically, outbreaks of trench fever have been documented in modern times, particularly among vulnerable populations. For example, outbreaks have occurred among injection drug users in Seattle, Washington, and Baltimore, Maryland, in the United States, as well as in Marseille, France, and Burundi. The natural history of trench fever is generally not fatal, but complications can arise in some cases. Persistent fever may lead to heart failure, and long-term effects can include neurasthenia (a condition characterized by fatigue and weakness), cardiac disturbances, and muscle pain (myalgia). The clinical presentation of trench fever typically involves a relapsing fever that lasts for five days, although continuous fever is rare. The incubation period is relatively long, averaging about two weeks. Symptoms often begin suddenly and include high fever, severe headache, pain with eye movement, muscle soreness in the legs and back, and heightened sensitivity (hyperaesthesia) of the shins. The initial fever is usually followed by a brief fever spike after a few days, and there may be multiple relapses interspersed with fever-free periods. The most consistent symptom is leg pain. Recovery from the illness can take a month or longer. Laboratory diagnosis of trench fever often relies on serological testing, such as the Weil-Felix test. However, these tests are typically effective only after symptoms have been present for about a week. Treatment for trench fever primarily involves antibiotics from the tetracycline group, such as doxycycline or tetracycline, which are administered for seven to ten days. In cases where tetracycline derivatives are contraindicated—such as in patients with severe liver or kidney dysfunction, children under nine years of age, or pregnant women—chloramphenicol is recommended as an alternative. For patients with bacillary angiomatosis, a related condition caused by Bartonella quintana, erythromycin is the treatment of choice and is typically administered for three to four months.
